steps.user_message: I'm preparing my 2024 taxes and could use your help. Situation: married filing jointly, Phoenix AZ. W-2 from Acme Corp: $82,350. Side income: $11,200 from web design (3 clients). Interest $2,340 (Chase savings), dividends $440 (Robinhood). Home office: 110 sq ft, rent $1,600/month, apartment 780 sq ft. Deductions: student loan interest $4,400 (Sallie Mae, 2017–2020); charity $1,100 to Boston Medical Center (donation, have receipt) with receipt; unreimbursed expenses $950. Can you help me figure out deductions, standard vs itemized, and home office treatment—and which forms to use?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Thanks — I can walk you through this and give a rough calculation so you can see whether itemizing makes sense, how to treat the web-design income and the home office, and which federal (and state) forms you’ll use. I do need two quick clarifications (below) before finalizing numbers, but here’s a clear, actionable overview and an initial estimate.

Quick clarifying questions
- The “student loan interest $4,400 (Sallie Mae, 2017–2020)” — is that interest you paid in tax year 2024, or is that total interest you paid across 2017–2020? For the federal student loan interest deduction you can only deduct interest paid in the tax year you’re filing for (and you should have a 1098-E for that year). If it’s $4,400 paid in 2024 we’ll also need to check the AGI phaseout for the deduction.
- Any other possible itemized items not listed? (Mortgage interest, property tax, state income tax withheld, large medical expenses, etc.)
- Any business expenses for the web-design work besides the home office (software, hosting, equipment, advertising, contractor costs, mileage, etc.)?

High-level summary / recommendations
- Income to report on your 2024 federal return:
  - W-2 wages: $82,350 (Form W-2)
  - Interest: $2,340 (Form 1099‑INT)
  - Dividends: $440 (Form 1099‑DIV)
  - Self-employment (web design) gross: $11,200 — report on Schedule C; subtract business expenses (including the home-office portion if you use the regular method) to get net profit.
- Self-employment tax and forms:
  - Report business on Schedule C (Form 1040). Self-employment net profit flows to Form 1040 and is subject to self-employment (SE) tax.
  - Compute SE tax on Schedule SE (Form 1040). You can deduct half of SE tax as an adjustment to income on Schedule 1.
  - If you use the regular home-office method, use Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) to calculate the allowable home portion. If you use the simplified method, you do not use Form 8829.
- Home-office: regular method likely gives the larger deduction here (details below).
- Student loan interest: this is an above-the-line deduction (Schedule 1) up to $2,500 (subject to MAGI phaseout). Not an itemized deduction.
- Unreimbursed employee expenses: generally NOT deductible for 2018–2025 under federal law (TCJA), so the $950 is likely not deductible unless you fall into a very narrow exception.
- Charitable: $1,100 is an itemized deduction only (with a receipt). If your total itemized deductions are less than the standard deduction, take the standard deduction.
- Standard vs. itemized: For 2024 the standard deduction for Married Filing Jointly is $29,200 (confirm when you prepare return). With only $1,100 of charitable donations listed (and no mortgage interest/property tax numbers provided), you will almost certainly take the standard deduction. So likely standard deduction > itemized.

Home-office deduction — which method to use and numbers
You have 110 sq ft home office, apartment 780 sq ft → business use percent = 110 / 780 = 14.10%.

Annual rent = $1,600 × 12 = $19,200.

Two methods:

1) Simplified method
- $5 per sq ft up to 300 sq ft = 110 × $5 = $550
- Easy recordkeeping; no Form 8829.
- This reduces your Schedule C business income by $550.

2) Regular method
- Business portion of rent = 14.10% × $19,200 ≈ $2,708
- If you have utilities or renter’s insurance, you can also allocate those the same way and add them; that increases the deduction.
- Use Form 8829 to calculate and transfer to Schedule C.
- This reduces your Schedule C business income by approximately $2,708 (plus any other allocated items).

Which is better here?
- Regular method is substantially larger (~$2,708) than simplified ($550). Based solely on rent, regular method saves you roughly $2,158 more of taxable income before SE effects. So regular method is likely the better choice (unless you prefer the simplicity of the simplified method).

Short example (estimate) — shows effect of using regular vs simplified home-office
Assumptions: no other business expenses; no student-loan interest claimed (or we’ll add it later once clarified).

A) Regular method
- Schedule C net profit: 11,200 − 2,708 = 8,492
- Net earnings subject to SE = 0.9235 × 8,492 ≈ 7,847
- SE tax ≈ 7,847 × 15.3% ≈ $1,199 ; half deductible ≈ $599
- Gross income before adjustments = W-2 82,350 + interest 2,340 + dividends 440 + Schedule C net 8,492 = $93,622
- Adjustments: half SE tax ≈ $599 (plus student loan interest if eligible)
- AGI (approx) ≈ $93,022
- Subtract standard deduction (MFJ $29,200) → taxable income ≈ $63,822

B) Simplified method
- Schedule C net profit: 11,200 − 550 = 10,650
- SE calculation: 0.9235 × 10,650 ≈ 9,839 → SE tax ≈ $1,505 ; half deductible ≈ $752.50
- Gross income = 82,350 + 2,340 + 440 + 10,650 = $95,780
- AGI after half SE tax (≈752.50) ≈ $95,028
- Taxable income ≈ $95,028 − $29,200 = $65,828

Difference (regular vs simplified) ≈ $2,006 lower taxable income using regular method in this rough example — so regular method saves tax and is likely worth the extra recordkeeping.

Student loan interest
- The federal deduction is an adjustment on Schedule 1 up to $2,500 (subject to MAGI phaseout). You must have a 1098‑E showing amounts of interest paid in the tax year. Clarify which year the $4,400 relates to; only interest paid in 2024 can be claimed on your 2024 return, and the max deductible amount is $2,500 (and may be phased out depending on MAGI). If you actually have $2,500+ paid in 2024 and your MAGI is low enough, you can claim up to $2,500.

Charitable
- $1,100 with a receipt — deductible only if you itemize. Since your likely itemized total is small, you’ll almost certainly take the standard deduction instead of itemizing.

Forms you will use (federal)
- Form 1040 (main form)
- Schedule 1 (additional income & adjustments) — for student loan interest deduction and other adjustments
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — report web-design income and business expenses
- Schedule SE — compute self-employment tax
- Form 8829 — if you use the regular method for the home office deduction (computes home-office portion)
- Keep (and attach if required by software) copies of 1099‑INT (interest), 1099‑DIV (dividends), 1099‑NEC (if you received for clients), and W‑2
- Consider Form 8995 / 8995‑A for QBI deduction (Qualified Business Income) — you may be able to claim up to 20% of qualified business income from your Schedule C. Because your QBI is relatively small and you’re MFJ, the QBI calculation should be straightforward, but confirm taxable income after deduction; tax software calculates this automatically.

State forms (Arizona)
- Arizona individual return: Form AZ Form 140 (or the appropriate AZ return for 2024). Arizona will start with federal AGI and then apply state modifications; include your federal schedules when preparing state return.

Other practical notes
- Keep records supporting the home-office square footage measurement and allocation of rent/utility bills. Keep receipts for charitable donation and 1098‑E for student loan interest (if you claim it).
- If you earned $11,200 as self-employment income and no or insufficient tax was withheld, you may owe income tax + SE tax; consider estimated tax payments for next year or increasing withholding on W-2.
- Unreimbursed employee expenses (the $950) generally are not deductible on federal return for 2018–2025.
- If you had business expenses for web design (supplies, software subscriptions, equipment), list them on Schedule C — they reduce SE and income tax.

Next steps I can do for you
- Recalculate with the student loan interest clarified and any additional business expenses / state tax amounts so the estimate is precise.
- Prepare a checklist of documents/1099s you’ll need for filing.
- If you want, I can draft a summary you can send to a CPA (or prepare a worksheet/estimate of tax owed) — tell me whether to use the regular or simplified home-office method for the final calculation.

Which of the clarifying items above can you answer now? I’ll update the numbers and give a final, line-by-line list of what to enter on each form.
